question: What evidence exists on how AI use affects different learner profiles — high vs. low performers, younger vs. older students, novices vs. experts?
answer:
**AI Use Across Learner Profiles: What the Evidence Shows**

The question of how AI tools affect different kinds of learners — sorted by prior achievement, age, or expertise — is one of the most consequential in contemporary educational research. The emerging picture is neither uniformly optimistic nor uniformly alarming, but it is distinctly uneven: the same tool can be a scaffold for one learner and a crutch for another, and the distinction tracks, with uncomfortable regularity, along existing lines of advantage.

**High vs. Low Performers**

Among the clearest findings to emerge from recent longitudinal work is that high-achieving students are adopting AI more strategically and more quickly than their lower-performing peers. The percentage of the highest-performing students — those earning 80 percent or above — who use AI both as a tool and as a facilitator more than doubled from 5.4 percent to 11.3 percent in just one year, according to a large study tracking over 26,000 K–12 students in Michigan Virtual's online courses. Meanwhile, achievement analysis demonstrated a learning curve effect, where the initial performance gap between AI users and non-users narrowed substantially within one year, with higher-achieving students showing an over 111 percent increase in sophisticated AI usage.

This trajectory might seem to suggest convergence, but the mechanism matters. The cognitive risks of detrimental offloading are not distributed equally. Students who already possess strong domain knowledge and metacognitive skills are better placed to use AI beneficially: they offload the right things and keep the hard work for themselves. Students without those skills are more susceptible to detrimental offloading. They fall prey to the illusion of competence and bypass the learning they need most. Some analysts have called this the "Matthew Effect" for an AI-mediated world — the already-rich get richer. While the cognitive offloading paradox affects all learners, it is particularly damaging for already-struggling students; for them, frictionless AI is not acting as an equalizer but is instead widening existing achievement gaps by denying them the opportunity to encode material that is crucial for achieving mastery.

The performance paradox at the heart of this problem is now well-documented. A growing body of empirical research provides clear evidence for a "performance paradox": AI can boost a student's performance on an immediate task while simultaneously diminishing the durable learning that is the actual goal. High-quality prompts show forethought, contextual detail, and clear specifications, while low-quality prompts rely on the AI to fill in gaps, reflecting weaker planning and monitoring. High-performing students iteratively refine prompts, demonstrating productive evaluative judgment. The implication is that the student most at risk of being harmed by AI assistance is the one whose prior knowledge is too thin to evaluate what the AI is producing.

**Younger vs. Older Students**

Age introduces a different set of gradients. Adoption rates rise sharply with grade level: a little under a quarter of students in grades 11 and 12 (24 percent) report using ChatGPT, compared with 17 percent in grades 9 and 10 and 12 percent in grades 7 and 8. Among adolescents, there is also a clear age-related pattern in how AI is used rather than merely whether it is used. A higher percentage of older teens (16 to 18) than younger teens (13 to 16) used AI to summarise texts (45.5 percent vs. 31.5 percent) or to provide different interpretations of a text (19.1 percent vs. 10.1 percent). This suggests that older adolescents deploy AI for more cognitively demanding, interpretive tasks, while younger ones are more likely to use it for basic retrieval or completion.

A study on adolescents and generative AI found strikingly different adoption rates across age groups within secondary schooling: among younger adolescents (mean age 14), approximately 14.8 percent reported using generative AI, while among older adolescents (mean age 17), the adoption rate rose to 52.6 percent. The concern about passivity is not confined to older students, however. While roughly half of young people report adding their own thoughts to AI outputs, one in four admitted to simply copying AI outputs when using it for homework — a figure that increased from 20.9 percent in 2024 to 25.1 percent in 2025.

A broader study across age groups — not limited to school settings — found that younger participants aged 17 to 25 exhibited higher AI tool usage and cognitive offloading, but lower critical thinking scores. This association does not establish causation, but it reinforces the hypothesis that intensive AI use during formative years of cognitive development may carry particular risks. While 80 percent of high school educators report that their students are receiving formal AI literacy lessons, only 8 percent of students in Pre-K through 3rd grade are receiving the same training, creating a significant developmental gap in early childhood education.

**Novices vs. Experts**

The novice-expert distinction is arguably where the research is most theoretically grounded, and where the policy implications are sharpest. Cognitive science has long established the "expertise-reversal effect": instructional strategies beneficial for novice learners can actually impede learning for more experienced students — a finding with direct implications for AI tutoring systems, where a one-size-fits-all approach may be counterproductive.

The good news for novices is that AI tutoring, when well-designed, can genuinely close skill gaps. In a randomized clinical trial in medical education, both the AI tutor and the human tutor groups demonstrated significantly superior performance compared to the control group across all primary outcome measures, and crucially, no statistically significant differences were found between the AI tutor and human tutor groups on any performance metric. For novice medical trainees, AI-driven tutoring was as effective as expert human instruction for acquiring foundational laparoscopic skills and superior to self-learning, validating AI tutors as a viable and scalable tool to complement traditional expert feedback.

The picture darkens, however, when novices encounter general-purpose AI rather than pedagogically scaffolded systems. Experts benefit more than novices from AI collaboration and rely on stronger skills in task decomposition and evaluation of AI outputs; in code comprehension, experts inspect data more deeply, verify assumptions about transformations, and navigate outputs with clear goals — behaviors that novices underuse. Studies also document failure patterns such as "prompting rabbit holes," where less-experienced users iterate on prompts without convergence.

Novices benefit from worked-out examples that make the solution rationale explicit, whereas more advanced learners benefit from prompts that elicit self-explanations, allowing them to complete solution steps on their own. This pedagogical distinction — historically managed by skilled human teachers — now falls to AI systems that are often not designed to detect or respond to it. Context-aware AI tutors that adapt their level of guidance based on student expertise could theoretically provide more effective support across diverse skill levels, avoiding excessive scaffolding for advanced learners while maintaining necessary support for beginners — but most commercially available tools do not yet achieve this reliably.

## AI and Differential Learner Profiles: Who Benefits, Who Doesn't, and Why

The question of whether AI tools help all students equally has attracted serious empirical attention over the past two years, and the emerging answer is clearly no. The effects of AI on learning vary significantly across performance levels, age groups, and prior expertise — and the patterns are more complex, and more cautionary in places, than the technology's advocates tend to acknowledge.

### High vs. Low Performers

One of the most consequential findings concerns the divergence between high and low performers. The promise of AI tutoring is that it can rescue students from classes "pitched to the median" in which high-achieving learners are insufficiently challenged while struggling students fall behind. There is genuine evidence for this potential: lower-performing students, specifically those one standard deviation below the mean, showed meaningful improvements — an additional 0.15 SD gain on state tests — when human-AI hybrid tutoring was compared to AI-only tutoring. Yet the same research found a troubling wrinkle: lower-performing students showed lower AI tutor use than their higher-performing peers, suggesting that the students most in need of the tool are also the least likely to engage with it consistently.

Meanwhile, studies on language learning point in a similar direction. In a study of English language learning in Nigeria, those who gained the most benefit from generative AI access were higher academic achievers, implying that AI may amplify, rather than reduce, existing performance gaps. In writing contexts, AI's impact varies by students' independent writing competence, with lower-proficiency students potentially struggling to leverage AI effectively. The tool, in other words, rewards those who already bring enough prior skill to use it well.

Design matters enormously here. In a randomized controlled trial with roughly 1,000 high school mathematics students, AI-assisted performance improved by 48%, but unassisted exam performance fell by 17% relative to control — a stark reversal suggesting that when students use AI as an answer machine rather than a thinking partner, short-term task performance comes at the cost of durable learning. Research by Bastani et al. indicated that although generative AI instantly enhanced students' problem-solving performance, these benefits diminished or became negative by final examinations, with participants' end-of-term grades declining when AI was available without pedagogical guardrails.

A counterpoint comes from research on AI-assisted human tutors. Students whose tutors used AI assistance were 4 percentage points more likely to progress through math tutoring assessments successfully, with the approach particularly benefiting lower-rated and less-experienced tutors — students of lower-rated tutors who used AI assistance increased their math proficiency by up to 9 percentage points on average. The implication is that AI's greatest leveling potential may lie not in replacing human instruction but in elevating the quality of weaker instructors.

### Novices vs. Experts

The novice-expert divide reveals a distinct cognitive mechanism. Research highlights systematic differences between novices and experts when collaborating with AI for programming: in agent-based modeling, experts could benefit more than novices, relying on stronger skills in task decomposition and evaluation of AI outputs; in code comprehension, experts inspect data more deeply, verify assumptions, and navigate outputs with clear goals — behaviors that novices underuse. Novices, lacking the mental scaffolding to evaluate AI outputs critically, risk being led astray rather than guided forward. Studies also document failure patterns such as "prompting rabbit holes," where less-experienced users iterate on prompts without convergence.

The underlying danger for novices is well captured by the metacognitive dimension: while a ChatGPT-assisted group showed improved task performance during the supported intervention phase, there were no differences in posttest knowledge gain or knowledge transfer, and a temporal process analysis suggested that the ChatGPT group relied strongly on AI support and showed relatively low metacognitive processing compared to other support groups. For novice learners specifically, the negative impact of large language models on the depth of inquiry was found to be "particularly true for novices." Programming research extends this concern: a novice programmer who relies on a tool like GitHub Copilot may learn how to prompt the AI but not how to think like a programmer.

That said, the novice case is not uniformly bleak. Using AI code generators can significantly increase task completion, improve correctness scores, reduce errors, and reduce task completion time for novice programmers during training. And crucially, learners with higher prior programming competency performed significantly better on retention tests if they had access to the AI code generator during their training phase — a finding that once again underscores how prior knowledge moderates the benefit.

### Younger vs. Older Students

Age-based differences in AI use are well documented, though research on differential *learning outcomes* by age remains thinner than research on adoption patterns. A higher percentage of older teens (16 to 18) than younger teens (13 to 16) used AI to summarize texts (45.5% vs. 31.5%) or to provide different interpretations of a text (19.1% vs. 10.1%), suggesting that older adolescents are both more aware of and more sophisticated in their AI use. Adoption within schools also scales with grade: nearly a quarter of students in grades 11 and 12 (24%) reported using ChatGPT, compared to 17% in grades 9 and 10 and 12% in grades 7 and 8.

Critically, engagement quality diverges as much as usage rates. More young people who enjoyed reading or writing added their own thoughts to AI outputs, while those who did not enjoy these activities were more likely to copy AI responses directly — a gap that was especially pronounced around reading enjoyment. This suggests that motivation and existing affinity for a subject mediate how productively students of any age interact with AI tools.

### The Overarching Pattern

What emerges across all three dimensions — performance level, expertise, and age — is a consistent dynamic that researchers have begun to call the *assistance-erosion paradox*: AI raises immediate performance while potentially undermining the deeper cognitive work that produces lasting knowledge. While AI offers rapid access to information, overdependence may reduce students' engagement in independent analysis and reflective reasoning; when used reflectively and with appropriate regulation it may serve as a tool for intellectual stimulation, but excessive or passive AI use may impair the very skills it aims to enhance. The students most at risk of passive use — lower performers, novices, and younger learners with weaker metacognitive skills — are precisely those for whom the stakes of that erosion are highest. Studies have only sporadically examined how individual characteristics moderate the impact of generative AI on learning outcomes, and a more well-rounded analytical framework has been lacking, meaning the field's understanding of these differential effects remains genuinely incomplete.

These are materially new data points that extend and enrich the answer. However, the core conclusions remain the same — AI benefits are unequally distributed, higher performers and experts gain more, novices and lower performers are at greater risk — so the verdict is B rather than C.
